faq.a: Whatever the contract says, which is why ownership and data rights should be agreed before development.
If their outputs feed regulated decisions, yes; for exploratory research, lighter controls may apply.

An assistant responds to a request and waits. An agent pursues a goal across several steps and uses tools, which means it can take actions in other systems, so it needs explicit limits on what it may do.

reading.body:
Drugmakers are co-developing AI agents that sit inside research platforms as scientist assistants, with Owkin building such agents under a multiyear collaboration with Sanofi.

The pattern is co-development rather than procurement. A research organisation does not buy a finished agent and install it. It builds the agent alongside a specialist AI company, inside its own platform, so the agent works on internal and public data, runs analyses, and suggests next steps to scientists. That arrangement puts the agent close to the science rather than beside it.

The governance questions follow from that closeness. Who owns the agent and the improvements it learns from company data is a contract term, not a default. Whether the partner can reuse what it learns with other clients is a second term. Where outputs feed regulated decisions, validation applies; exploratory research may carry lighter controls. None of this is settled by the technology itself.

The data covers one named collaboration and the questions it raises. It does not give costs, timelines, headcount, or measured results, so it cannot show whether these agents work or what they return. It also says nothing about the compute and power behind them, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

explainer:
Research organisations are building AI agents that work inside their own platforms: searching internal and public data, running analyses, summarising results and suggesting next steps for scientists. Some are developed with specialist AI companies under multiyear collaborations.

Co-development raises questions worth settling first: who owns the agents and the improvements they learn from company data, whether the partner can reuse anything with other clients, how data are protected, and how the agents will be validated where their outputs feed regulated work.

How agents differ from assistants

An assistant answers a question and stops. An agent is given a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools such as document stores, lab systems or scheduling software, and keeps going until the goal is met or it hits a rule that says stop. In a research organisation that difference matters, because an agent that can read a protocol can also, if allowed, file a change request, book instrument time or send a query to a site. Every one of those actions needs a decision about whether the agent may do it alone, do it with a person approving, or never do it.

Where agents are being tried first

The early uses are the ones where the steps are well defined and the cost of a mistake is low or easily reversed: assembling literature packs, drafting first versions of standard documents, reconciling data between two systems, triaging support tickets, and preparing meeting summaries with action items. Lab in the loop work, where an agent proposes the next experiment and a scientist decides, is the most ambitious use and the one with the least settled evidence.

What a responsible rollout looks like

Start with a written list of what the agent may touch, which systems it may write to, and which actions always need a named person. Log every action the agent takes in a form a quality auditor can read. Give it a budget of time, money and API calls, and make it stop when the budget runs out rather than improvise. Review the logs weekly for the first months. Treat each new permission as a change that needs its own risk assessment, the same way a new user role would in a validated system.
